entries.title: United States: developers plan a record 86 GW of new capacity in 2026
entries.summary: EIA's generator inventory shows US developers planning 86 GW of new utility-scale capacity for 2026, more than any year on record if it all happens.
points: Planned 2026 additions: 43.4 GW solar (51%), 24 GW battery storage (28%), 11.8 GW wind (14%) and 6.3 GW natural gas.
For comparison, EIA reports 53 GW of new capacity in 2025 in total, with 27.2 GW solar and a record 15 GW of battery storage.
More than half of the planned solar is in four states: Texas (40%), Arizona (6%), California (6%) and Michigan (5%).
These are plans reported by developers, not installed capacity; projects slip or are cancelled.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: the pipeline for 2026 is mostly solar and batteries, but a pipeline is not a finished build.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding.

entries.title: Great Britain: the Smart Export Guarantee pays small solar owners for exported power
entries.summary: Under Ofgem's Smart Export Guarantee (SEG), some electricity suppliers must pay small generators for low-carbon electricity they export to the grid. Each supplier sets its own rate, and the rate must be above zero.
points: The SEG launched on 1 January 2020 and is government-backed.
It covers installations up to 5 MW (50 kW for micro-CHP) using solar PV, wind, micro-CHP, hydro or anaerobic digestion, located in Great Britain.
SEG licensees (the suppliers) decide the rate, contract length and other terms. Payments are based on export meter readings.
Because rates differ by supplier, Ofgem tells generators to shop around.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: if you export solar power in Great Britain, check several SEG tariffs; they are not all the same.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. This entry does not list current tariffs.

entries.title: European Union: the 2030 renewable energy target is at least 42.5%, aiming for 45%
entries.summary: The revised Renewable Energy Directive (EU) 2023/2413 sets a binding EU-wide target of at least 42.5% renewable energy in gross final consumption by 2030, with an aim of 45%.
points: The amending directive entered into force on 20 November 2023, with 18 months to transpose most provisions and a shorter deadline of July 2024 for some permitting rules.
It adds sector targets for heating and cooling, transport, industry and buildings, and binding targets for renewable fuels of non-biological origin.
It also speeds up permitting, for example through shorter approval periods and 'renewables acceleration areas'.

The Commission's page states that renewables were 26.2% of EU energy consumption and 47.2% of EU electricity production in 2025, and that proposals for a post-2030 framework are planned by the end of 2026.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: the EU's 2030 goal is to roughly double the renewable share of its energy, and the rules are set at EU level but carried out by each country.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. National rules and progress differ by country.

entries.title: Germany: new solar systems face a 60% feed-in limit until a smart meter is fitted, and no feed-in payment at negative prices
entries.summary: Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG 2023) sets technical rules for small solar systems and removes the payment basis during negative wholesale prices. The official statute text sets the numbers.
points: Section 9(2) EEG 2023: until a smart metering system and control box are installed and tested, solar systems under 25 kW that receive the feed-in tariff must limit grid feed-in to 60% of installed capacity; systems of 25 kW to under 100 kW must be remotely controllable (and, if on the feed-in tariff, also limited to 60%); systems of 100 kW or more must be remotely controllable.
Plug-in solar devices up to 2 kW with an inverter of up to 800 VA are excluded from these technical requirements.
Section 51(1) EEG 2023: for periods when the spot-market price is negative, the 'applicable value' used to calculate the payment is reduced to zero.

Section 51(2): this does not apply to systems under 100 kW until the end of the calendar year in which a smart metering system is installed, nor to systems under 2 kW until the end of the year after the Federal Network Agency makes a specified determination. Section 100(47) lets operators of older plants opt in.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: in Germany a new small solar system's export is capped at 60% until it has a smart meter, and exports at negative prices can earn nothing.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. Which rule applies depends on the system's size, commissioning date and tariff type; the statute has transition rules this summary does not cover.

entries.title: Australia: the Cheaper Home Batteries discount became smaller for larger batteries on 1 May 2026
entries.summary: The federal Cheaper Home Batteries Program gives about a 30% discount on small batteries (5 to 100 kWh). Since 1 May 2026 the certificate factor falls every six months and tapers with battery size.
points: The discount comes from small-scale technology certificates (STCs) based on usable capacity; households do not apply to the government, and installers or retailers pass it on, or owners can claim STCs themselves.
STC factor: 8.4 (January to April 2026), 6.8 (May to December 2026), 5.7 (January to June 2027), falling to 2.1 by the second half of 2030.

Since 1 May 2026 the factor applies at 100% for the first 14 kWh, 60% for kWh above 14 up to 28, and 15% for kWh above 28 up to 50. No extra certificates above 50 kWh, although batteries up to 100 kWh remain eligible.
The government says it expanded the program from an estimated $2.3 billion to $7.2 billion over four years, and the Clean Energy Regulator administers it.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: the support per kilowatt-hour is higher for the first 14 kWh and lower for bigger batteries, and it steps down over time.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. Eligibility and the discount value depend on the installation date and the Regulations.

entries.title: Japan: the 7th Strategic Energy Plan aims for about 40-50% renewables in the power mix by FY2040
entries.summary: Japan's 7th Strategic Energy Plan (February 2025) projects renewables at about 40-50% of electricity in fiscal 2040, up from 22.9% in fiscal 2023, and treats renewables as a major power source alongside nuclear.
points: FY2040 outlook: renewables about 40-50% (solar about 23-29%, wind about 4-8%, hydro about 8-10%, geothermal about 1-2%, biomass about 5-6%), nuclear about 20%, thermal about 30-40%.
FY2023 preliminary figures in the same document: renewables 22.9% (solar 9.8%, wind 1.1%, hydro 7.6%), nuclear 8.5%, thermal 68.6%.
Electricity generation is expected to be about 1.1 to 1.2 trillion kWh in FY2040, against 985.4 billion kWh in FY2023.
Policy directions include a perovskite solar cell target of 20 GW by 2040, floating offshore wind in the exclusive economic zone and next-generation geothermal.
The plan gives ranges from several scenarios because of uncertainty; they are outlooks, not forecasts of a single result.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: Japan's plan roughly doubles the renewable share of its electricity over about 15 years and keeps nuclear in the mix.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. The figures are policy outlooks with wide ranges.

entries.title: India: PM Surya Ghar pays up to Rs 78,000 towards a home rooftop solar system
entries.summary: As approved by India's Union Cabinet in February 2024, PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana gives central financial assistance for residential rooftop solar, aimed at one crore (10 million) households.
points: Assistance is 60% of system cost for the first 2 kW and 40% of the additional cost between 2 and 3 kW, capped at 3 kW.
At the benchmark prices then used, that is Rs 30,000 for 1 kW, Rs 60,000 for 2 kW and Rs 78,000 for 3 kW or more.
Households apply through the national portal and choose their own vendor; collateral-free loans at around 7% (at the time) were available for systems up to 3 kW.
The Cabinet outlay was Rs 75,021 crore, targeting 30 GW of residential rooftop solar and free electricity up to 300 units a month for participating households.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: the scheme covers a share of the cost of a home rooftop system up to 3 kW, and you apply on the government portal.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. The amounts are those announced in 2024; benchmark prices and scheme terms may have changed since.

entries.title: Netherlands: net metering for solar ends on 1 January 2027
entries.summary: The Dutch salderingsregeling, which lets solar owners offset exported power against what they use, ends on 1 January 2027. After that, suppliers must pay a compensation for exported power instead.
points: Until 31 December 2026 households and small businesses can offset the electricity they feed back against their yearly use, with no energy tax on the offset amount.
From 1 January 2027 offsetting is no longer allowed, but owners can keep feeding power into the grid and receive a payment from their supplier.
Until 2030 that payment must be at least 50% of the supplier's bare electricity supply tariff, which is the price without taxes.
Suppliers often charge feed-in costs too; these may only cover the supplier's own costs of handling the exported power, and the consumer authority ACM supervises them.
entries.plain_tip: In plain terms: from 2027 Dutch solar owners are paid for exports, but the old one-for-one offset against their own use goes away.
entries.caution: Summary of an official publication, not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules and figures change; check the official page and local rules before deciding. Actual payments and feed-in costs differ by supplier.
